newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Smugglers pack Albanians in two boats for Italy.
newsitem.headline: Smugglers pack Albanians in two boats for Italy.

text.p: An organised gang smuggling Albanians out of their troubled homeland has attempted to send two crowded ships to Italy in the past 24 hours, a spokesman for a multinational security force in Albania said on Sunday.
Over 1,200 Albanians are believed crammed onto the two vessels.

The first set sail from Velipoje Beach, 30 km (20 miles) south of Shkoder in northern Albania late on Saturday, undetected by Italian navy vessels. It was due to arrive at Bari in southern Italy at 1500 GMT with up to 700 people on board.
Details about the second vessel were not so clear but an Italian coastguard spokesman said it was believed to still be in Albanian waters after leaving from near Velipoje.
"The multinational force is not at present deployed in this area so we could not prevent the departures," spokesman Lieutenant Colonel Giovanni Bernardi told Reuters.

"At Vlore (in southern Albania), traffic of illegal immigrants is no longer active with troops securing the port. Maybe the traffic from the north could stop when the multinational force is deployed there in the next two weeks."
Security sources in Tirana said the first vessel had been bought in Montenegro for $120,000 by a gang based in northern Albania that is organising the lucrative traffic of illegal immigrants.
Albanians desperate to flee the impoverished Balkan nation pay about $500 each for a place on a boat.
The Italian coastguard does not have the authority to stop boats carrying illegal immigrants and can only warn the captain to turn around or face arrest on arrival in Italy.
Thousands of Albanians have fled to Italy or Greece in the past three months since a wave of violence spread across Albania after the collapse of popular, high-risk savings funds.
With some of the 6,000 soldiers of the eight-nation force deployed at the key ports of Vlore and Durres, unsecured Velipoje has become a favoured launch point.
Last Sunday Italian authorities at Barletta rescued 571 Albanians packed into an ageing vessel built for 50 that had left from Velipoje, taking 26 hours to limp its way to Italy.
The conditions in which Albanians are transported are appalling and there have been tragic consequences.
An estimated 103 people drowned on March 28 when an overcrowded ship from Vlore in southern Albania collided with an Italian navy frigate 30 miles off Brindisi and sank.

This is the second time that Albanians have fled en masse from their Balkan home which is Europe's poorest country with many of the 3.4 million people living in poverty, exacerbated by the funds disaster that erased an estimated $1.2 billion.
A huge number emigrated illegally to Italy and neighbouring Greece in 1991 and 1992 after the collapse of a ruthless Stalinist government which ruled for 46 years.
The current crisis in Albania exploded when protesters angered over the loss of savings took to the streets, blaming President Sali Berisha for not taking action against the funds.
As law and order collapsed, Albanians raided military arsenals, taking up arms for self-protection or for criminal purposes. An estimated 700 people have died since February.
